newsitem.title: UK: Rifkind attacks UK Labour over EMU stance.
newsitem.headline: Rifkind attacks UK Labour over EMU stance.

text.p: Labour's apparent readiness to sign up for a European single currency in 2002 if it has proved to be a success by then is an "absurd proposition," Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday.

Rifkind told a news conference a Conservative government would decide whether it was in Britain's national interest to join in light of what economic and monetary union (EMU) meant for jobs, national security, standards of living and prosperity.
For Robin Cook, Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, to make a decision to join dependent on whether the machinery of EMU was working was at best "an extraordinarily superficial approach."
"We would apply a far more rigorous test and it is one the British public would expect us to take," Rifkind said.

He said Labour's willingness to surrender the national veto in some areas was weakening Britain's negotiating hand in the running inter-governmental conference (IGC) on how to streamline the European Union's institutions.

"I cannot hide from you that Labour's public concession of so many important negotiating objectives of other European countriess is undermining Britain's negotiating position in the IGC," Rifkind said.

Rifkind listed the minimum consequences of what he said was Labour's willingness, as set out in policy documents and speeches by party leaders, to sign the Social Chapter and accept qualified majority voting in social, environmental, industrial and regional affairs.
He said Labour, without a veto, would be impotent to resist:
-- an endless stream of social legislation.
-- the loss of up to 1.6 billion pounds that Britain receives from the EU's regional fund.
-- the imposition of an alien town-and-country planning system that could impinge on Britain's right to protect the environment.
-- directives to Britain's power generators on the fuels they must use, resulting in much more expensive electricity.
"The consequences of what we know about Labour's policies would be expensive and painful," Rifkind said.
